questions.title: How does the Tenth Circuit review a single-member BIA affirmance and when can it rely on the IJ’s reasoning?
questions.question_body: The opinion says it reviews the BIA’s decision but can consult the IJ’s “more complete explanation” (citing Uanreroro). Here, a single BIA member affirmed and the panel repeatedly leans on the IJ’s findings. What are the limits on this practice? If the BIA’s short decision didn’t expressly adopt every IJ ground, can the court still rely on those IJ rationales under substantial-evidence review, or must the BIA have clearly incorporated them?

questions.title: Why weren’t armed threats and the attempted grabbing of the child enough to constitute past persecution?
questions.question_body: The panel emphasizes that “threats alone are insufficient,” but the facts include two men holding Jimenez at gunpoint, later assaulting an employee while searching for the family, and a man putting his arm around the son and covering his mouth. The court notes petitioners conceded no lasting physical harm. In Tenth Circuit asylum law, how are incidents like being held at gunpoint or an apparent attempted abduction treated—are these still categorized as mere threats absent injury? What factors tip such episodes into “persecution” when aggregated?

questions.title: Did the court properly apply the mixed-motive ‘one central reason’ test given both the political leaflet and the ‘snitch’ accusations?
questions.question_body: Petitioners received a brochure saying “death to snitches from Liberal Party,” and the men later called them snitches and linked them to the prosecutor’s office, while also saying the order came from Don Rafa. The court concludes the predominant motive was Jimenez’s interference with Don Rafa’s criminal enterprise, not politics. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(i), how should a court weigh evidence of both political animus and personal/economic motives? Does the leaflet explicitly tying politics to being a “snitch” support an imputed political opinion theory, and if so, why was that not enough to satisfy “at least one central reason”?

questions.title: What level of reporting to authorities is required to prove the government is ‘unable or unwilling’ to protect, and does speaking with two officers suffice?
questions.question_body: The opinion stresses the lack of formal reporting and cites a Seventh Circuit case about avoiding reliance on a single unhelpful officer. Here, petitioners spoke to two officers, one of whom told them police were contributing to the problem and advised them to leave. In the Tenth Circuit, is this kind of informal notice enough to show the state had an opportunity to respond? What evidence is necessary to establish futility or danger from reporting when the persecutor is allegedly tied to political actors, especially where the record also shows prior police search attempts?

questions.title: Who bears the burden on internal relocation when there is no finding of past persecution, and did the panel apply the correct standard?
questions.question_body: The court says even if petitioners had a fear of future persecution, they could reasonably relocate within Colombia, citing family safety and a prior three-week stay in the countryside. Under 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(3), when the alleged persecutor is a private actor and there’s no past persecution, the applicant usually bears the burden to show relocation is unreasonable. Did the panel analyze the regulatory reasonableness factors (e.g., ongoing risk, social ties, access to work, government reach), or was it enough to point to family members’ safety and the assailants’ demand to leave only the neighborhood?

questions.title: Was any ‘particular social group’ claim forfeited, and could a PSG like ‘perceived informants to law enforcement’ be viable in the Tenth Circuit?
questions.question_body: The court limits the nexus analysis to political opinion because petitioners did not brief PSG. Does failing to brief a PSG theory to the BIA or on petition for review forfeit it entirely? Substantively, has the Tenth Circuit recognized (or rejected) PSGs based on being informants, witnesses, or perceived “snitches” to law enforcement, provided particularity and social distinction are shown? If such a PSG were pursued, what evidence would be needed to meet those requirements in Colombia?

questions.title: When does opposition to criminal organizations or corruption count as a ‘political opinion’ for asylum purposes?
questions.question_body: The persecutor here is described as a guerrilla/narco leader allegedly aligned with the sitting president. The court characterized the motive as economic retaliation for interfering with a criminal enterprise, not political opinion. In Tenth Circuit doctrine, when can anti-corruption activity, cooperation with prosecutors, or opposition to criminal groups be treated as an actual or imputed political opinion, rather than a personal or economic dispute? What additional facts would typically be necessary to tilt this into the political-opinion category?

questions.title: Why did withholding of removal ‘necessarily’ fail once asylum failed, and are there scenarios where withholding could still succeed?
questions.question_body: The panel concludes that because petitioners failed to show a well-founded fear for asylum, they necessarily fail the higher standard for withholding. I understand withholding has a higher likelihood-of-persecution standard but different bars and no discretion. In what circumstances could a petitioner be denied asylum yet still prevail on withholding (e.g., one-year bar, discretionary denial, firm resettlement), and why were those not in play here? Also, since the children were derivative on asylum, does the analysis change for them on withholding, which does not allow derivatives?
